li.a: AAP: Notorious prison escapee's legal bid for freedom fails (20 November 2025)
AAP: 'Postcard Bandit' in legal bid for freedom from WA jail (17 June 2024)
Hunter Valley News (AAP): Captured prison escapee asks court for freedom (1 July 2025)
Government of Western Australia: Minister refuses interstate transfer of notorious criminal Brendon Abbott
Fremantle Shipping News: So, it's all about Brenden Abbott, the 'Postcard Bandit' (19 June 2025)
Fremantle Prison: Escape Stories in the Modern Era

content.p: Brenden James Abbott became a household name in Australia in the 1980s, according to a 2025 broadcaster's announcement. He was dubbed the "Postcard Bandit". He was convicted of armed robbery and escape offences, escaped from two prisons, and spent years on the run. In November 2025 the Supreme Court of Western Australia largely rejected his bid to have his detention declared unlawful. He remains in custody in Perth, and in 2025 a six-episode television drama based on his story was commissioned.
content.h2: Fremantle Prison in the years before his escape
content.p: Fremantle Prison, in Perth, began as a convict establishment and was later modified to stop escapes. The prison's own history of escapes says the building was altered with gun towers and reinforced perimeter walls with razor wire, yet breakouts continued. The institution says escape attempts from the prison were "numerous, frequent and often successful".

The same history records a garbage-truck escape on 24 March 1989, when two prisoners on sick parade seized a truck, rammed the south wall gates and led police on a chase across Perth's southern suburbs. The prison's account says the escape changed security afterwards, with bollards and steel ropes added inside and outside the gates. The two men named in that account were Stephen Burnett and Peter Boyd, not Abbott.
content.h2: The 1980s robberies and the first escape
content.p: A 2025 announcement from the Foxtel Group and its Binge streaming service described Abbott as a figure who "became a household name" in the 1980s through a string of bank robberies, evading police, and then being arrested, convicted and escaping custody twice. The same announcement said that, apart from inmates convicted of murder, he was then the longest-serving prisoner in Australia. That is the broadcaster's own claim.

Western Australia's government, in a ministerial statement to parliament, said Abbott was a ringleader in the Fremantle Prison riot of January 1988. He had been on remand for other offences at the time, and the government said he was sentenced to six years for the riot, in addition to the 10 years he had received for the offences he was on remand for.

In November 1989 he escaped from Fremantle Prison. The state statement says that during the next five years he committed a number of armed robberies. AAP reported that in 2017 he received a concurrent five-year term for the 1989 escape.
content.h2: Arrest on the Gold Coast and the 1997 escape
content.p: Abbott was arrested on the Gold Coast in March 1995, about five and a half years after the Fremantle escape. AAP reported that he was suspected of robbing banks in Western Australia, South Australia and Queensland of up to $5 million. No court finding on that total is reported.

The state statement says he was taken into custody in Queensland in 1995 and found guilty of crimes committed there. He was held in the Sir David Longland prison in Brisbane. In November 1997 he escaped from that prison, while serving a sentence for the Gold Coast bank robberies, according to AAP. The state statement says that after the escape he committed three armed robberies in Queensland and one in Western Australia before he was apprehended in Darwin.

The same statement gives the Queensland sentence as 24 years, seven months and seven days. It lists four counts of armed robbery, along with escaping custody, serious assault, taking a vehicle without authority and breaching the Prisons Act. The figure comes from that statement.

AAP reported that Abbott was recaptured in Darwin in May 1998. He then served about 18 years in Brisbane prisons before he was extradited to Perth in May 2016 to serve the Western Australian sentence, according to the AAP reports.

Before that, the state's Corrective Services Minister, Margaret Quirk, told state parliament that she had refused his request to move to Western Australia. Abbott had applied on welfare grounds, because his mother lived in the state. Quirk said his son and the son's mother lived in New South Wales, and his girlfriend was in Queensland. She said she was not convinced that a transfer served the prisoner's welfare. She also cited security concerns and what she called "a string of victims across the country and particularly here in WA", and noted that Abbott was wanted in South Australia for offences there.
content.h2: The 2024 challenge in the Supreme Court
content.p: In June 2024 Forbes Kirby Lawyers filed judicial review proceedings in the Western Australian Supreme Court to challenge his sentence. As AAP reported it, Abbott claimed that the sentencing laws brought in during November 1996 were not applicable to him, and that his Western Australian custodial sentence had lapsed while he was in custody in Queensland. He also challenged the constitutional validity of the laws requiring a returned escapee to serve an extra period equal to one-third of the time he was at large. He claimed that imposing a sentence without a court's intervention "offends" the separation of powers.

His lawyers said the matter could ultimately end up before the High Court. He said the question was "the constitutional power the state has to keep people in prison after their sentences end". He added: "Views will differ about that, just like they did about Ned Kelly 150 years ago."

AAP also reported that Abbott was classed under a High Security Escort classification. That meant he was held in maximum security and could not be considered for a self-care unit or for the prison's resocialisation program, which the report said was generally reserved for inmates serving life sentences. The report said prison authorities regarded him as an escape risk, although there had been no escape attempt since his 1998 recapture.
content.h2: The 2025 ruling and the sentence dates
content.p: In November 2025 Justice Amanda Forrester of the state's Supreme Court largely rejected his claims. AAP reported her words: "The applicant has been largely unsuccessful." She said the constitutional argument "was misconceived from the start." She also said some of his arguments were misguided and irrelevant.

The court did reduce his maximum term, but it extended his parole eligibility date. The court ruled that he must serve 4,508 days from 12 April 2016. On that basis his sentence finishes on 6 November 2030, and he becomes eligible for parole on 15 August 2028. AAP noted that he had earlier been eligible for parole on 23 October 2026, with a maximum term expiring on 12 January 2033. His lawyer said the client was likely to appeal.

The 2024 AAP report had said that Abbott was technically eligible for parole in October 2026, but that he might never be granted it, and would stay in custody until the maximum term ended in January 2033. The two reports are from different dates, and the 2025 ruling is the later account.

At a court hearing reported on 1 July 2025, Abbott's son James spoke to AAP outside the court. "If you do the crime, you do the time," he said. "But the amount of time that dad has done for what he's done is more than enough." He added: "He's paid his debt to society and he deserves to spend time with his family."
The family's view is one side of the case. In November 2025 the Supreme Court largely did not accept his arguments.
content.h2: The book and the television drama
content.p: The drama is based on Derek Pedley's book, Australian Outlaw – The True Story of Postcard Bandit Brenden Abbott. In June 2025 Binge commissioned a six-episode, one-hour series, announced by the Foxtel Group, produced by Warner Bros. International Television Production Australia and distributed by ITV Studios. George Mason was announced as the lead, with Robyn Malcolm, Ashleigh Cummings and Keiynan Lonsdale in supporting roles. The announcement said filming was taking place in Western Australia, and the state's film agency, Screenwest, said the production was expected to spend more than $7 million in the state's economy.

The announcement describes the series as inspired by the true story. A drama is not a court record, and it does not establish any fact that the court rulings and government statements above do not. Readers who want the detail of the cases should look at the court rulings and the government statements above.

No result of any appeal after November 2025 is reported. The amount he was suspected of stealing is given as "up to $5 million" in AAP's reporting, with no court finding on the total. The Queensland sentence figure comes from an earlier government statement, and the later sentence figures come from 2025 reporting, so the two should not be combined as a single current total. The name is spelled "Brenden" in AAP reporting and "Brendon" in the government statement.
